body.statement: If \(\Theta_I(q;\delta_D,\delta_S)\) is nonempty, then it is the attained closed interval \([L(q;\delta_D,\delta_S),U(q;\delta_D,\delta_S)]\), even when the infimum of \(H\) over compatible positive-denominator laws is zero.  For each unscreened orientation having a positive-\(H\) feasible point, the two branch endpoints are obtained by the normalized programs in \(\mathrm{def:normalized\text{-}endpoint\text{-}program}\), and the same programs certify absence of a positive-\(H\) point otherwise.  After the observable residual-capacity direction screen, at most \(2^{r_{\rm amb}+1}\) linear programs are required.  These programs have rational data whenever \(q\), \(\delta_D\), and \(\delta_S\) are rational.
body.justification: The result handles vanishing denominators without trimming the model and turns an exponential branch count into a data-adaptive exact count.
body.gap: Linear-fractional response-law formulations are known, but no adjacent result proves endpoint attainment and scalar connectedness for this disjunctive minority-budget class.
body.consumer: Applied researchers obtain one interpretable sharp interval at every sensitivity pair, with no arbitrary lower cutoff on the always-selected-complier share.
body.proof_tex:
Fix an orientation \(o\) and abbreviate its compact polytope by \(Q_o\).  Compactness follows directly from the diagonal upper bounds by \(q\), the residual equalities, and \(0\leq n_x\leq h_x\leq\min\{U_x,V_x\}\).  We first prove a denominator-safe polytope fact.  Every point of a compact polytope is a convex combination of its finitely many vertices: indeed, in the minimal face containing a nonvertex point, extend a line through that point to the two boundary points of the face and induct on face dimension.  Finiteness follows because a vertex is determined by a full-rank subset of the finite constraint list.

Write a point as \(z=\sum_j\alpha_jz^j\), where the \(z^j\) are vertices.  Since the branch restrictions imply \(0\leq N(z)\leq H(z)\), a vertex with \(H(z^j)=0\) also has \(N(z^j)=0\).  If \(H(z)>0\), then
\[
 \frac{N(z)}{H(z)}
 =\sum_{j:H(z^j)>0}
 \frac{\alpha_jH(z^j)}{H(z)}\frac{N(z^j)}{H(z^j)},
 \qquad
 \sum_{j:H(z^j)>0}\frac{\alpha_jH(z^j)}{H(z)}=1.
\]
Thus a positive-denominator branch has a positive-denominator vertex, and its smallest and largest ratios are attained at such vertices.  Conversely, mixing its two endpoint vertices gives a positive denominator and, by continuity of the displayed ratio along the segment, every intermediate value.  Each nonempty branch image is therefore an attained closed interval.  This argument is unaffected by a sequence with \(H\downarrow0\).

The normalized program is exact.  A point \(z\in Q_o\) with \(H(z)>0\) maps to
\[
 y=z/H(z),\qquad \lambda=1/H(z),
\]
and satisfies all of its constraints with objective \(N(z)/H(z)\).  Conversely, a normalized feasible pair cannot have \(\lambda=0\): the homogenized diagonal upper bounds then force every diagonal coordinate to zero; the homogenized residual equalities force \(u,v,r,s,c,f\) to zero; and \(h_x\leq U_x,V_x\) then forces \(H=0\), contradicting \(\eta y=1\).  Hence \(z=y/\lambda\in Q_o\), \(H(z)=1/\lambda>0\), and the objective is the same ratio.  The positive-denominator endpoint vertices found above map to feasible normalized optima, so unboundedness of \(\lambda\) when denominators approach zero does not prevent objective attainment.

We next establish scalar connectedness across orientations.  Let \(\mathcal D\) be the set of diagonal arrays satisfying the diagonal bounds, residual balance equations, and defier budget.  It is convex.  For \(d\in\mathcal D\), put
\[
 h_x^star(d)=\min\{U_x(d),V_x(d)\},\qquad
 H^star(d)=\sum_xh_x^star(d),\qquad
 B_x^star(d)=\min_kB_{xk}(d).
\]
The function \(H^star\) is concave because it is a sum of minima of two affine functions.  Hence
\(\mathcal D_+=\{d\in\mathcal D:H^star(d)>0\}\) is convex.

Starting from any feasible reduced point with \(H>0\), first move each \(n_x\), within its cut interval, to
\[
 n_x^ell(d,h)=\max\{0,h_x-B_x^star(d)\}.
\]
Then increase \(h_x\) linearly to \(h_x^star(d)\), retaining
\(n_x=n_x^ell(d,h)\).  The lower selection bound remains satisfied, the ordinal cuts remain satisfied by the ordinal-cuts lemma, and \(H\) stays positive.  Moreover the actual minority mass
\[
 \sum_x\bigl(\min\{U_x,V_x\}-h_x\bigr)
\]
decreases along this path, so the maintained budget continues to hold.  This connects the original point to the canonical point
\[
 \bigl(d,h^star(d),n^ell(d,h^star(d))\bigr).
\]
For two canonical points, join their diagonals by a line segment in \(\mathcal D_+\) and evaluate the same canonical formulas along it.  The functions involved are finite minima and maxima of affine functions, hence continuous; the resulting path remains feasible, has zero minority mass, and has positive \(H\).  The full positive-denominator reduced feasible set is therefore path connected.  By the projection--lifting theorem its ratio image is the causal identified set, and a continuous image of a path-connected set in \(\mathbb R\) is an interval.  The already-proved finite-branch endpoint attainment makes it the closed interval \([L,U]\).

Finally, the promised screen is observable and safe.  Write \((a)_+=\max\{a,0\}\), and define
\[
 \underline f_x=\max\left\{
  \sum_{w\in\mathcal V}(q^1_{x0w}-q^0_{x0w})_+,
  \sum_{w\in\mathcal V}(q^0_{x1w}-q^1_{x1w})_+
 \right\},
 \qquad
 \overline f_x=\min\left\{\sum_wq^1_{x0w},\sum_wq^0_{x1w}\right\}.
\]
The coordinate bounds for \(r\) imply
\(r_{xw}\in[(q^1_{x0w}-q^0_{x0w})_+,q^1_{x0w}]\), and the analogous bounds for \(s\) imply
\(s_{xw}\in[(q^0_{x1w}-q^1_{x1w})_+,q^0_{x1w}]\).  A box of coordinate intervals realizes every total between the sum of its lower endpoints and the sum of its upper endpoints.  Intersecting the two total intervals therefore proves that the exact pre-minority feasible range is
\(f_x\in[\underline f_x,\overline f_x]\).  Nonemptiness of the target implies
\(\sum_x\underline f_x\leq\delta_D\).  Consequently every feasible point obeys
\[
 f_x\leq \operatorname{cap}_x
 :=\min\left\{\overline f_x,
 \delta_D-\sum_{y\ne x}\underline f_y\right\}.
\]
Define the observable selected-state contrast
\[
 g_x=\sum_{i\in\mathcal Y}(q^0_{x0i}-q^1_{x0i})
     -\sum_{j\in\mathcal Y}(q^1_{x1j}-q^0_{x1j}).
\]
Direct substitution of the residual definitions gives
\[
 U_x-V_x=g_x+\sum_{i\in\mathcal Y}r_{xi}
                 -\sum_{j\in\mathcal Y}s_{xj},
 \qquad |U_x-V_x-g_x|\leq f_x.
\]
Thus \(g_x\geq\operatorname{cap}_x\) guarantees \(V_x\leq U_x\) at every feasible point, while
\(g_x\leq-\operatorname{cap}_x\) guarantees \(U_x\leq V_x\).  Fix the corresponding smaller-margin orientation in every such cell.  Dropping the other orientation loses nothing: its branch budget uses the larger nonnegative quantity and hence its feasible points are already feasible under the smaller-margin choice.  If \(r_{\rm amb}\) cells remain, there are at most \(2^{r_{\rm amb}}\) branches and two normalized endpoint programs per branch, or \(2^{r_{\rm amb}+1}\) programs.  Their coefficients are rational whenever the supplied masses and budgets are rational.
